title: What Is Biblical Inerrancy? The Spectrum of Views
subtitle: The Chicago Statement, infallibility, and limited inerrancy. What the battle for the Bible was actually about.
triageNote: The total trustworthiness of Scripture stands very near the foundation. Every position on this page claims to be defending it. The fight is over the right word for that trustworthiness and how far down into the details it reaches. That fight split seminaries, denominations, and friendships across the twentieth century. That is exactly what a second-order issue does. It divides faithful churches without dividing the faith. The people on every side of this page pray to the same Lord. Each would tell you the Bible will not fail you. Learn what they actually disagree about before you decide whose side you were on all along.
question: Inerrancy is the claim that Scripture, in everything it affirms, is without error. That includes its statements about history and the world, not only faith and morals. Infallibility, as its advocates use the word, is the claim that Scripture will never fail or deceive in what it was given to teach, the way home to God. Its incidental details speak the ordinary language of their time. Limited inerrancy splits the difference with a scalpel. Inerrant in everything revelational, everything that matters for doctrine and salvation. Humanly fallible in the incidentals. All three camps say the Bible is true. The question is what the word true is doing. And whether a Bible that could err about the small things you can check can still be trusted about the large things you cannot.
whyItMatters:
In 1976 Harold Lindsell published a book called The Battle for the Bible. It named names. It argued that every institution which gave up the word inerrancy eventually gave up much more. Fuller Seminary had removed inerrancy from its statement of faith in 1972. After a decade of internal struggle. In 1978 some three hundred scholars and pastors gathered in Chicago and produced the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy. Nineteen articles of affirmation and denial. They remain the touchstone definition. In 1979 Jack Rogers and Donald McKim answered with a five-hundred-page argument that the church's central tradition had never taught the Princeton doctrine in the first place. In 1982 John Woodbridge answered them. In 1983 the Evangelical Theological Society pressed Robert Gundry to resign over his commentary on Matthew. Its entire doctrinal basis was at the time one sentence about inerrancy. This was not a seminar discussion. Careers ended. Schools split. Families chose churches over it.

And underneath the institutional fighting sits a question that finds every reader eventually, usually at night. You hit your first hard discrepancy. Matthew's Jeremiah where Zechariah seems intended. The mustard seed that is not in fact the smallest of all seeds on earth. The numbers in Kings that do not match the numbers in Chronicles. What do you do now. One camp tells you the difficulty is apparent, not real. Giving an inch here costs the whole Bible eventually. Another tells you the difficulty is real and harmless. Precision in incidentals was never what God was promising you. A third tells you to sort what is revelational from what is not. Your answer will shape how you read and how you defend the faith. It will shape what happens to you the next time a documentary tells you the Bible is full of errors.

positions.name: Full inerrancy, the Chicago position
positions.inOneLine: Scripture, in its original manuscripts and rightly interpreted, is wholly true in everything it affirms, because its primary author is the God who cannot lie. That includes history and science as well as faith.
positions.bestCase:
My argument has three steps and the first two are not controversial among Christians. God cannot lie. Scripture says so in so many words, it is impossible for God to lie. And Scripture is God's word, breathed out by Him. The third step refuses to let the first two pass without their consequence. If the Bible is God's word and God cannot err, the Bible does not err. To say otherwise is to say either that God errs or that some of the Bible is not really His. I have never seen a third option that was not one of those two wearing a coat.

Now let me tell you what I am not claiming. This position is rejected most often in versions no signer of the Chicago Statement ever held. The Statement's thirteenth article denies that inerrancy is negated by a lack of modern technical precision, by irregularities of grammar or spelling, by observational descriptions of nature. By reports of falsehoods spoken by others, by round numbers, by topical arrangement, by free citations. The sun rises in an inerrant Bible. That is true ordinary speech. The mustard seed is the smallest seed a Galilean farmer sowed. Jesus was speaking proverbially to farmers, not writing botany. Inerrancy attaches to what the text, read by the rules of its own genre, actually affirms. Establish what Matthew is affirming. I will defend that affirmation to the end. I am not required to defend what a hostile reading or a wooden reading puts in his mouth.

Why hold the line at the hard cases instead of conceding a few errors in the incidentals. Because of who taught me my doctrine of Scripture. Jesus said Scripture cannot be broken. He staked an argument on one word of a psalm. He treated Jonah, the flood, and Adam as real. If I say the Bible errs in things that can be checked, I am correcting the One I call Lord on the nature of the book He submitted to. And because of where the other road goes. It is not slippery-slope rhetoric, it is observed history. The method that surrenders the Bible's accuracy in geography in one generation is applied to its miracles in the next. Then to its morals in the third. Because it is the same method. The interpreter stands over the text deciding which parts carry authority. Warfield's image holds. The trustworthiness of Scripture is a seamless garment. There is no such thing as cutting carefully.

One more honest word about the original manuscripts. We attach inerrancy to the autographs, the texts as given, not to every copyist's slip in the long transmission. Critics call this a dodge, since no autographs survive. It is not a dodge, it is a definition. We can establish the original wording to a very high degree. The science of textual criticism exists for exactly that. Where a number has been garbled in copying, the garble is the copyist's, not the Spirit's. No doctrine of any consequence hangs on a disputed reading. The distinction between what God breathed and what scribes did with it is as old as the scribes.

positions.name: Infallibility for faith and practice
positions.inOneLine: Scripture is the wholly trustworthy word of God that cannot fail in what it was given to do, teach the way of salvation and the life of faith. Its incidental details belong to the human languages and eras God stooped to use.
positions.bestCase:
I want to begin with a historical claim. My position is routinely treated as the new and eroding one. I do not accept that framing. Rogers and McKim argued in 1979, and whatever you make of every detail of their case, this much stands up. When Augustine and Calvin and the Westminster divines confessed Scripture's perfection, the perfection they had in view was its saving purpose. Calvin speaks of God lisping to us as a nurse lisps to a child, accommodating Himself to our capacity. He handles the small discrepancies of the evangelists without alarm. The tight definition of inerrancy as technical accuracy in all details, defended with the apparatus of harmonization, is characteristically a nineteenth-century Princeton formulation. It was honed in a fight with modernism. It is a respectable position. It is not the only old one, and mine does not descend from unbelief. It descends from the doctrine of accommodation.

Now the word itself. Infallible is not a softer word than inerrant, it is a stronger one aimed at a different target. Inerrant means contains no mistakes. Infallible means cannot fail. I claim the second for Scripture, and I mean it absolutely. The Bible cannot fail you in anything it was given by God to teach you. Who God is. What He has done in Christ. How you are forgiven. How to live and die. On that terrain it is not merely accurate, it is invincible. What I decline to claim is that the Bible settles, or intends to settle, the kinds of questions a modern fact-checker brings to it. The precise order of events that the evangelists themselves arrange differently. The standing of numbers that ancient historiography handled conventionally. The cosmology its writers shared with their neighbors. God did not correct Isaiah's astronomy before giving him the gospel of comfort. The astronomy was never the message.

Here is my deepest problem with the tight formulation, and I say it as a friend. It quietly relocates your faith. The full inerrancy position, lived out, makes the trustworthiness of the gospel hang on the success of harmonization. So somewhere a believer is white-knuckled over whether the cock crowed once or twice, feeling the resurrection itself wobble. That is a cruelty no one intended. It comes from promising on the Bible's behalf something the Bible does not promise about itself. Scripture nowhere offers you a doctrine of its own technical precision. It offers you a God who does not lie about the things He is telling you. Berkouwer taught me to let Scripture's authority be the authority it actually exercises. The God-breathed power to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. That is Paul's own sentence about what the sacred writings are for. I am content to claim everything Paul claimed. And nothing he did not.
advocates: Jack Rogers and Donald McKim (The Authority and Interpretation of the Bible, 1979)

positions.name: Limited inerrancy
positions.inOneLine: Scripture is inerrant in everything revelational, all that it teaches for doctrine, salvation, and life. Its non-revelational incidentals, matters of science and minor history, can reflect the human limits of the writers.
positions.bestCase:
I hold the least comfortable seat at this table, fired at from both sides. So let me make the case with some care. I came to it by exegesis, not by compromise.

Start with 2 Timothy 3:15-16, and read the two verses together, in order. The sacred writings are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable, for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness. Daniel Fuller's point, which convinced me, is that Paul himself states the scope of Scripture's purpose before he states its inspiration. The scope is revelational, the knowledge that makes you wise for salvation and equipped for every good work. I therefore affirm, without a tremor, that in everything the Bible was given to reveal, it is without error of any kind. God's character, the covenants, the incarnation, the atonement, the resurrection, the commands, the promises. Test me anywhere on that ground. I will defend the text against all comers.

But I decline to extend the divine guarantee to assertions that lie outside that purpose, the incidental furniture of the revelation. Because I think the text itself declines to. The Bible's statements about the natural world are the statements of its centuries. Its minor historical details sometimes sit unevenly beside each other, and beside the records of the ancient world. In ways that two thousand years of harmonization have managed rather than removed. The full inerrantist handles each case with a separate tool, here a round number, there a copyist, here a genre, there a paraphrase. I respect the labor. But at some point the number of tools is itself the evidence. My account needs one tool. God's revelation came through real first-century and Iron Age people. Where they touched matters God was not revealing, they wrote as the careful, honest, limited people they were. The treasure is intact. The vessel is earthen. Paul said both.

What do I say to the slippery-slope charge, that my distinction hands the reader scissors. I say the scissors exist on every view. Mine at least tells you where the cutting line is, fixed by Paul's own statement of purpose, not by my preferences. The revelational content of Scripture is not a canon within the canon that I select. It is everything the text teaches, asserts, and demands about God, humanity, and salvation. Which is to say, nearly everything in it. What falls outside is the kind of thing no creed ever confessed and no soul ever needed. The seed's exact rank among seeds. The precise overlap of two royal chronologies. I am not grading God's word. I am refusing to make promises in its name that it never makes, and then watching students lose their faith when the promises fail. I have seen that happen. It is why I am here.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God never lies, and it is impossible for God to lie. The premise of the inerrantist syllogism in its plainest form. Whatever God says is true, because of who is speaking.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for no one as stated, which is the point of contention. All three views affirm it and deny that it settles the question. The issue is not whether God lies but what, in Scripture, God is asserting.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Full inerrancy reads it as closing the case: every affirmation of Scripture is God's, so every affirmation is true. Infallibility answers that God's truthful speech comes accommodated to human idiom. A father using his child's words is not lying. Limited inerrancy answers that the verse guarantees everything God is teaching. The debate is over the scope of the teaching, which this verse does not address.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus, arguing from a single phrase of Psalm 82, says in passing that Scripture cannot be broken. He treats the precise wording of an obscure verse as carrying unbreakable authority. That is the inerrantist instinct exactly.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for infallibility and limited inerrancy. The Lord's own casual confidence extends to a detail, a single word in a psalm, not to a broad saving message.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility answers that cannot be broken means cannot be annulled or fail of its purpose, the language of authority, not of technical precision. It notes that Jesus is making a point about what Scripture calls people, a revelational matter. Limited inerrancy agrees. The verse shows Scripture's teaching authority is indefeasible, and a psalm's statement about judges is teaching. Neither side grants that the verse addresses incidental historical detail.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Infallibility and limited inerrancy as evidence of human texture
biblicalEvidence.summary: Matthew attributes to Jeremiah a prophecy whose wording comes substantially from Zechariah 11:12-13. The most discussed attribution difficulty in the New Testament. On the page of an evangelist writing under inspiration.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for full inerrancy, which must explain why an inerrant text names Jeremiah where the words are Zechariah's.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Full inerrancy offers serious answers, not evasions. Matthew signals a composite citation, since the field, the potter, and the price draw on Jeremiah 19 and 32 as well as Zechariah. And ancient citation practice named the more prominent prophet, as Mark 1:2-3 cites Isaiah for a blend of Isaiah and Malachi. Infallibility finds the explanation possible but strained. It asks why a free citation under ancient conventions is not simply admitted as such, an ordinary human practice God did not override. Limited inerrancy reads it as a textbook non-revelational incidental. The theological claim, that the betrayal price fulfilled prophecy, stands either way.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Infallibility and limited inerrancy as evidence of human texture
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says David entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence. In 1 Samuel 21 the priest is Ahimelech, Abiathar's father. This verse is the one that moved the inerrancy debate at the Evangelical Theological Society more than once.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for full inerrancy, since the apparent misnaming sits in the recorded words of Jesus.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Full inerrancy answers that the Greek phrase epi Abiathar can mean in the passage about Abiathar, the section-heading use found elsewhere in Mark. Or in the days of Abiathar, the more famous priest who was present and shortly became high priest. Infallibility regards those readings as available but motivated. It sees a Lord who spoke with the historical shorthand of his day, his point, mercy over ritual, untouched. Limited inerrancy files it with Matthew 27:9, an incidental that no doctrine ever rested on. The instinct to defend it at all costs is the theory's demand, not the text's.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Numbers reports twenty-four thousand dead in the plague at Peor. Paul says twenty-three thousand fell in a single day. A small, famous, checkable difference inside the canon itself.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a definition of inerrancy that demands modern numerical precision. Useful to every side for showing what the biblical writers themselves counted as faithful reporting.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Full inerrancy resolves it without strain. Paul specifies in one day, Numbers gives the whole plague, or both use round numbers, which Chicago's Article XIII explicitly allows. Infallibility agrees with the resolution and draws the moral. The writers' own standards of accuracy were conventional, not technical. That is all infallibility ever claimed. Limited inerrancy draws the same moral one step further. The Spirit was content with ancient counting conventions. The count was never the revelation.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Claimed as the charter by all three
biblicalEvidence.summary: The sacred writings make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view to claim exclusively, which is why it appears in every camp's opening argument. It states inspiration's fact, scope, and purpose in three sentences that each side accents differently.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Full inerrancy stresses all Scripture, every word God-breathed, therefore every affirmation true. Infallibility stresses the stated purpose, wise for salvation, equipped for good works, as defining the trustworthiness in view. Limited inerrancy reads the purpose clause as fixing the scope of the guarantee itself. The verse is the debate in miniature. That is worth knowing before anyone quotes it at you as a settled point.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver refined seven times. Every word of God proves true. Scripture's own celebrations of its verbal purity, in the strongest language the Hebrew has.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for views that locate trustworthiness in message rather than wording, since the texts praise the words themselves.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility answers that purity in these texts is covenant reliability, words that do not deceive or fail the one who takes refuge in them. The verse in Proverbs finishes with exactly that image, a shield to those who trust him. Limited inerrancy adds that every word proving true is the language of promise-keeping. God doing what He said, not a statement about incidental data. Full inerrancy replies that reliable words which contain errors is not a sentence the psalmists would have recognized.

weighing:
My judgment, held tentatively, one pastor thinking aloud.

I notice first how much smaller the disagreement becomes when each side is read carefully. Chicago's qualifications, taken seriously, concede round numbers, free citation, observational language, genre, and topical arrangement. That covers a large share of what the infallibilist wanted protected. The infallibilist, read carefully, claims absolute trustworthiness for everything Scripture teaches. That covers nearly everything the inerrantist was defending. The two sides' worked answers to Mark 2:26 are often within a sentence of each other. A great deal of the twentieth-century bloodshed was over the flag, the word inerrancy, in an institutional war where flags mattered. I want to be honest that flags sometimes do matter. And honest that a flag is not the territory.

Where do I land. I confess Scripture's total truthfulness. I find I trust the instinct of full inerrancy more than its apparatus. The instinct, that I do not stand over this book correcting it, that what it affirms, God affirms, is the posture Jesus models. I will not adopt a posture toward Scripture that my Lord did not have. But the apparatus, the long shelf of harmonizations each more ingenious than the last, sometimes defends the theory at the cost of the text's own manner. And the infallibility men are right. A faith trained to need every difficulty dissolved is a faith one stubborn difficulty from collapse. I have buried enough doubts with people to know this. The believer who was promised a Bible with no rough edges meets his first rough edge alone, at two in the morning. And feels lied to. Whoever taught him that the gospel hangs on the cock crowing once rather than twice did him no kindness.

So I would say it this way, tentatively. The Bible, in everything it affirms, tells the truth. Learning what it affirms is the labor of a lifetime. And the rough edges are nearly always sitting precisely where the affirmation is not. I hold the word inerrancy without embarrassment. And without making it the first word I say about Scripture. The first word is the one Paul chose: these writings are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Everything else on this page is guard rails for that road.
charitableDisagreement:
Know what each camp is protecting before you fire at any of them. The full inerrantist is protecting the principle of authority, having watched institutions that loosened the word loosen everything behind it within a generation. His fear is not paranoia, it is institutional memory. The infallibilist is protecting the actual texture of the Bible and the actual faith of believers. He refuses to chain the resurrection to the success of harmonization. The limited inerrantist is protecting honesty, the willingness to say in public what the difficulties are. He has watched students discover them unprepared and conclude the whole faith was a cover-up. Each of these is love for the same book wearing different work clothes.

Is it a hill to die on. The complete trustworthiness of Scripture, its authority and its inability to fail those who stake their lives on it, sits close enough to the foundation. I will contend for it anywhere. But the vocabulary, inerrant against infallible against inerrant-in-purpose, has been made a shibboleth too many times. Men have been sorted into faithful and suspect by their preference among words the Bible itself uses of itself never. Ask better questions of a teacher than which flag he flies. Ask whether he sits under the text or over it. Ask what he does when the text contradicts him. A man can sign the strictest statement and wiggle out of every verse that crosses his politics. And a man can decline the word inerrancy and submit to Scripture like a soldier to orders. The posture is the test. The rest is vocabulary. Vocabulary is worth debating and not worth dying over.

relatedDebates.note: Inerrancy is downstream of inspiration. The verbal-plenary model issues naturally in full inerrancy, the dynamic model in message-infallibility, the encounter model in reliability of witness. If the debate on this page feels stuck, the disagreement usually lives one page back. In the model of how God gave the book.

Every careful inerrancy statement attaches to the original manuscripts, which no one possesses. How close our copies bring us to those originals is the province of textual criticism, treated in this set under the manuscripts page. It matters to every position here.

The 2010s version of this debate concerned genre: if ancient biography compressed time and arranged events topically, is that error or convention. The discussion around Michael Licona's work on the Gospels, which cost him a position in 2011, replayed the older battle on new ground. It remains live.
